JSON: Name: primal_dual_ilqr_gpu_mpc Title: Primal-dual iLQR with GPU-parallel associative scan for real-time model predictive control of legged robots Short Hypothesis: Implementing a primal-dual iLQR solver using GPU-parallel associative scans and JAX-based vectorization reduces median per-iteration MPC solve time by at least 2x compared to acados and crocoddyl for prediction horizons N ≥ 50, and increases batched environment throughput by at least 10x, enabling stable closed-loop whole-body control at 50 Hz for single robots and centralized control for up to 16 robots. Related Work: Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) and its Gauss-Newton variant iLQR are widely used for robot MPC due to efficient Riccati-style backward passes but are traditionally single-shooting and sequential, requiring feasible initial guesses. SQP-based solvers exploit constraint handling and generality (e.g., acados) but scale linearly with horizon and cubically with state dimension. Recent GPU efforts either convert symbolic kernels to GPU code without control-flow support, rely on batched parallelism only, or accelerate QPs with methods that require offline precomputation; partial GPU iLQR implementations have parallelized some components but not achieved full logarithmic temporal scaling or exact backward passes. Existing approaches therefore remain limited by (1) incomplete exploitation of temporal and state-space parallelism, (2) CPU-GPU boundary overheads and offline precomputation requirements, (3) poor scaling for large state/control dimensions and centralized multi-robot problems, and (4) fragile inequality handling or loss of exactness in backward passes. Abstract: We address the computational bottleneck of nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) for legged robots by combining a primal-dual sequential quadratic programming formulation with a GPU-parallel associative-scan implementation of the Riccati recursion and a JAX-native implementation for full vectorization. The proposed method solves the primal-dual KKT system with logarithmic scaling in horizon length and squared-logarithmic scaling in state dimension, while preserving an exact backward pass and multiple-shooting formulation that tolerates infeasible warm starts. The main contribution is a practical, differentiable GPU solver that parallelizes temporally and across state/control dimensions, enabling real-time whole-body MPC at longer horizons and centralized MPC for multiple robots. Expected outcomes are substantially reduced per-iteration solve times, higher batched simulation throughput for learning-in-the-loop, and the ability to control more complex robot models (including whole-body dynamics) within real-time constraints. The implementation supports large-scale parallel experiments and permits end-to-end differentiability for integration with learning pipelines. Experiments: 1) Simulation environments: MuJoCo XLA and IsaacLab; dynamical models: Single Rigid Body Dynamics (SRBD) and Whole Body Dynamics (WB). 2) Hardware platforms: Unitree Go2 (quadruped) and Talos (humanoid) for selected closed-loop tests. 3) Baselines: acados (SQP), crocoddyl (DDP/FDDP), CPU-batched acados, Relu-QP-style GPU QP solvers, and a CPU single-shooting iLQR reference. 4) Metrics: median and 95% CI of per-iteration solve time (ms), wall-clock control latency (ms), iterations to convergence, optimality gap (relative cost vs baseline), dynamics constraint violation norm theta, closed-loop success rate (no fall/mission completion), real-time factor (simulated seconds per wall second), batched throughput (environments per second), GPU utilization and memory footprint. 5) Sweep variables and conditions: horizon lengths N ∈ {25,50,100,200}; state/control dimensionality: SRBD and WB single-robot; centralized multi-robot scaling with n ∈ {1,2,4,8,16} robots; batch sizes for learning throughput B ∈ {1,16,64,256,1024,4096}. 6) Ablations: (A) disable temporal associative scan (sequential Riccati), (B) disable state-space parallelization (single-run JAX), (C) single-shooting vs multiple-shooting, (D) remove JAX vectorization and run identical GPU kernels without batching, (E) vary inequality handling: relaxed barrier parameters μ ∈ {1e-2,1e-3,1e-4}. 7) Protocol: for each configuration run 30 randomized trials with randomized feasible and infeasible warm-starts, apply external disturbances (50 N, 0.25 s) at random times in 60 s episodes, record metrics. 8) Success criteria and comparisons: report median speedup vs acados and crocoddyl for N ≥ 50; report batched throughput improvement vs CPU-batched acados; analyze ablation impacts on solve time, constraint violation, and closed-loop stability. 9) Hardware measurement: repeat key configurations on an evaluation machine with Intel i7-13700KF, NVIDIA RTX 3080 and laptop RTX 4050 and report cross-device performance and compile/warmup times. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Numerical stability: parallel matrix inversions and small-batch GPU kernels can be sensitive to ill-conditioned Hessians or near-singular matrices, causing divergence or inaccurate updates. 2) Inequality handling: the relaxed barrier penalty may not enforce hard constraints tightly, producing constraint violations under aggressive maneuvers or contacts. 3) Line-search and convergence: filter/Armijo line-search implemented with fixed parallel alpha grids can fail to find acceptable steps in highly nonconvex WB problems, increasing iterations or rejecting feasible updates. 4) GPU-CPU overheads: for small horizons or low-dimension problems, GPU transfer and JAX compilation overheads can outweigh parallel gains making CPU solvers faster in those regimes. 5) Scalability limits: GPU memory capacity and parallel inversion complexity limit the maximum number of robots, horizon length, or batch size achievable in practice; runtime may degrade nonlinearly near hardware limits. 6) Generalization: performance measured on tested robot morphologies and contact patterns may not transfer to robots with large limb inertia fractions or highly coupled actuation without retuning cost/regularization. 7) Real-world safety: deployment on hardware introduces timing jitter, sensor noise, and unmodeled dynamics that can cause unsafe behavior if solver failures occur. 8) Reproducibility: JAX XLA compilation nondeterminism and differing GPU drivers can produce variance across systems.
